THE RILEY IMP

In the annals of British motoring history, few marques evoke the spirit of prewar sporting innovation as evocatively as Riley. Founded in Coventry, Riley established a reputation for advanced engineering and nimble handling—attributes that reached new heights in the early 1930s as the company pursued a sporting clientele. Among their most celebrated contributions stands the Riley Imp, unleashed in 1934 as a considerably lighter, shorter, and lower edition of the already revered Riley Nine.

Born of necessity and competition, the Imp was developed for enthusiastic drivers seeking an agile machine capable of both spirited touring and competitive motoring. Its coachbuilt two-seater roadster body, characterized by taut lines, a compact profile, and a delicately swept tail, captured the imagination of an emerging breed of sportsmen. Notably, the Imp weighed only 1,376 lbs, making it among the lightest in its class and bestowing it with a distinct performance edge.

Central to the Imp's enduring appeal is its jewel-like 1,087cc twin-camshaft, hemispherical-head four-cylinder engine. Meticulously engineered, Riley's unit employed twin camshafts set high in the block, actuating inclined valves; the engine's free-revving character and robust output defied its modest displacement. With twin SU carburetors and a sprightly 50 horsepower at its command, the Imp quickly established a reputation as a giant killer on both road and track.

The Riley Imp's advanced mechanical specification extended to its underpinnings, with an independent front suspension and a responsive, remote-control four-speed manual gearbox. Rigorous attention to balance and weight distribution made the Imp a favorite in trials, hill climbs, and endurance events, often besting larger-capacity rivals with grace. Drivers praised its precise steering, taut chassis, and willingness to reward expert hands with genuine driver pleasure.

Period acclaim soon followed, and the Imp's competition pedigree became legendary. Privateers and factory teams alike campaigned the model with distinction in such events as the Alpine Trial, the Ulster TT, and the Monte Carlo Rally. The Imp attracted not only racing accolades, but also the attention of connoisseurs—among them, future motorsport impresarios, successful industrialists, and enthusiasts with a penchant for technical excellence cloaked in elegance.

Surviving examples of the Riley Imp are among the most sought-after British sports cars of the prewar era. Their rarity, mechanical sophistication, and lithe bodywork ensure enduring desirability across generations of collectors. For those who value provenance as much as performance, few prewar roadsters offer a deeper association with motoring history and the golden age of English craftsmanship.

Today, the Riley Imp is loved not only for its rarity but for its engaging driving experience. Period road test reports, collected in publications such as The Autocar and Motor Sport, consistently praise the model's sprightly character, communicative chassis, and capability to devour country roads as few contemporaries could. The Imp encapsulates the best of prewar British engineering and remains, eight decades on, a coveted prize for discerning aficionados.

THE PLUS FOUR SUPER SPORTS

The Super Sports is the 'Holy Grail' of all Morgan production. The model took all of the sporting connotations that had been woven into the breed from its earliest days, reviving the 'Super Sports' title which they had applied to some of the most sporting three-wheelers, building on that heritage with the four-wheeled Plus Four Super Sports. In doing so, Morgan delivered legendary international racing success for the brand.

Not surprisingly, its story is linked to the greatest endurance race of all, the Le Mans 24 Hour Race. When Morgan racer and preparer Chris Lawrence elected to contest the 1961 running of this event, it is said that the organizers deemed a Plus Four to be a pre-war car and denied it eligibility. This move incensed Peter Morgan to such a degree that he agreed to provide full Works support for Lawrence, guaranteeing acceptance for the '62 edition. Lawrence brought his Super Sports home to a class win that year, earning the model its place in history and arguably perpetuating the company to this day. That car, known simply as 'TOK', referring to its British license plate number, led to production versions and countless replicas of the famed Super Sports.

As ever with Morgan, there was some variety and differentiation between the original Le Mans car and those that the public enjoyed, as customers sometimes chose specifications and the manufacturer worked to supply bespoke cars relative to their demand. As John Worrall and Liz Turner state in their book Original Morgan: "The Super Sports model was originally constructed with the standard Plus 4 body style, but with a bonnet scoop. These were the original high-line models. Later, however, the Super Sports models featured the same low-line body as the original 'Le Mans car'."

Worrall and Turner record that the production process saw the cars built with their running gear and ash frames. These were then sent to Chris Lawrence workshops in Westerham Motors. From here the engines, the clutch, flywheel, con rods and crankshaft were sent out to Jack Brabham Motors to be balanced. The cylinder head was polished and gas-flowed, and the compression ratio was raised to 9:1'. A high-lift camshaft was fitted, and then aspiration would come from 42 or 45 DCOE Webers mounted to a cast alloy manifold, a four-branch exhaust system ensuring clear exit. On the later, 'Low Line' cars, with the reduced height of the intake and exhaust set ups, the whole profile of the car was able to be lowered, and accordingly its radiator was cut down in height. While this aided the aerodynamics, the reduced radiator aperture had to be compensated for, which was achieved with a header tank set back on the firewall. A small bumper set was fixed to the front of the car while overriders only were fitted to its tail.

The combined effect of all of these improvements was to push the horsepower out from roughly 100bhp on standard TR4 engined cars to north of 125bhp, while its weight was shaved down from nearly 1,900lbs to 1,736lbs and allowed a 0-60mph of 7.6 seconds.

All told, production of the Super Sports tallied 101 cars only, a small fraction of the more than 4,500 Plus Four cars built. According to the Original Morgan book, among even this modest number some were more sporting than others, as a result of requirements offering one year guarantees on the enhanced specifications. Some arrived in this country un-tuned, and one was even delivered as a four-seater.


THE CAR OFFERED

Super Sports number 6388, as recorded in Morgan's own chassis record, was built new to left hand drive configuration and USA specification. Originally trimmed in Westminster Green over Black leather, the car was fitted with 72-spoke wire wheels, disc brakes, a wood-rimmed steering wheel, heater and defroster, rear bumper, and a badge bar with fog lights. Dispatched on December 20, 1966, it was retailed when new by Louwman & Parqui in Leidschendam, Holland – a break from their usual business of Dodges and Toyotas.

The Morgan was not long for the European continent and rather quickly made its way to the United States where documentation on file indicate it was originally purchased by of Gary Lee Webb in the New Orleans area. On September 24, 1985, Michael Norton of nearby Metairie, Louisiana acquired the Morgan for all of $1,000 and with a recorded odometer reading of 25,012 miles. A copy of the Bill of Sale from that transaction is on file. Retained briefly by Mr. Norton, the next known owner was Thomas Mossman who is reported to have bought the car later that same year. Kept for 23 years, in 2008 Peter Castner of Massachusetts became the penultimate owner with a reported 40,752 miles. The current owner purchased the Super Sport in April 2023 with 42,443 miles showing.

Service records on file go back some three decades with evidence of maintenance by marque specialists throughout. In March of last year the Plus Four was sent to the experts at Morgan Motors of New England in Copake, New York for an extensive mechanical overhaul that included service work to the fuel system, gaskets, motor mounts, steering, suspension, and more as well as a rebuild of the Weber carburetors. The total bill was over $6,400.

Driven about 1,200 miles in the current ownership, the records on file would tend to indicate that the nearly 43,650 miles on the odometer are likely from new. Reported to be largely original paint, the rear deck around the fuel filler was repainted in the current ownership. Currently fitted with a rare hard top, it is complete with a barely-used top and frame (not currently fitted to the car), interior tonneau cover, and side curtains. When shown at the Speed and Style Festival in Alexandria, Virigina in May of 2023, it was bestowed with the "Spirit of the Road" award.

Rarely does a Super Sport appear on the public market, such that they are perhaps occasionally overlooked for their sheer importance and eligibility. By the very nature of their broad international success roster in period, today it is possible to campaign one at numerous events, not least of course the Le Mans Classic.

THE ALFA ROMEO DUETTO SPIDER

Late in 1962, Alfa Romeo debuted the Giulietta's ostensible replacement - the Giulia. The power unit was the 1.6-liter, 109bhp version of Alfa Romeo's classic double-overhead-camshaft four as installed in the Giulia Sprint GTV. Performance fully matched the Duetto's stunning looks, with 60mph reachable in around 11 seconds and a top speed of 116mph.

A new Spider was launched in 1966. Designed by Pininfarina and penned by the founder himself, Battista "Pinin" Farina, it featured a rounded tail and emulated the famous 1952-53 "Disco Volante" race cars. At launch it had no specific name, but a company contest soon selected the name "Duetto." Pininfarina also manufactured the monocoque body, which was powered by the 1570 Giulia engine. The model gained its greatest fame by being cast in the 1967 Dustin Hoffman film The Graduate. So faithful was it's following that Alfa appended this name to the Series II North American version.

THE ESSEX SERIES A

While Henry Ford concentrated on his Model T to the exclusion of everything else other car manufacturers recognized there was a hierarchy of aspirations for style, performance and prestige. General Motors built a whole ethic about aspirational marques from Chevrolet to Cadillac.

Hudson, named for J.L. Hudson the Detroit department store magnate who funded the new marque of Roy Chapin and Howard Coffin, positioned itself as a premium marque almost from its inception in 1910. Hudsons became six-cylinder powered in 1913 and only looked back in 1919 when a more economical four-cylinder car made economic sense.

It was the Essex, a plainly Hudson-backed car that was presented as a new marque. The Essex offered a 179 cubic inch four (1919 Hudsons were 76hp 289 sixes) but with a difference: The Essex six used an F-head configuration with overhead intake valves and side exhaust valves in a shared offset combustion chamber. It cranked out 55 horsepower and delivered exceptional performance for its $1,395 price. Stodgily styled, the Essex was not pretty but its elemental design masked excellent performance and the late Teens and early Twenties market bought performance as is so often the case.

Coming from a collection with experience tuning similar machines for events such as The Great Race, this Essex was sympathetically restored and mechanically gone through some time ago, but has been kept in nice shape since. The engine has been complimented with a more modern alternator and distributor – all converted to 12 volt – for great reliability and easy of use. The rear end has been modified with a taller gearset, giving the car a higher top speed and more pleasant swift touring experience. Not used actively in recent years, a bit of recommissioning is recommended before any long distance driving, although the vehicle started and run well during an inspection by a Bonhams specialist.

With 55hp it has exceptional potential for tours and events and even with its Touring car body will upstage most of its contemporaries.

Powered by a modest yet reliable 1.2-liter flat-four engine, it offered straightforward mechanics and ease of maintenance, contributing to its enduring appeal. Its simple engineering and robust construction made it accessible and practical, securing its place as a cultural and automotive icon.

By 1967, the Beetle had refined its suspension and braking systems, balancing comfort with durability. The rear-engine layout and air-cooled design remained largely unchanged, emphasizing reliability over outright performance. Enthusiasts value this era for its authenticity and the tactile driving experience provided by the manual transmission and mechanical simplicity.

The Beetle's timeless design and mechanical honesty continue to attract collectors who appreciate its historical significance and the purity of its engineering. Its enduring popularity is supported by a strong community and availability of parts, making it a practical classic for both preservation and daily use.

THE JAGUAR XK120

Conceived and constructed in just a few months, the XK120 debuted at the 1948 Earls Court Motor Show where the stunning-looking Roadster caused a sensation, the resulting demand for what was then the world's fastest production car taking Jaguar by surprise. With orders rolling in apace, Jaguar had no choice but to think again about the XK120's method of construction. The body had been conceived as a coachbuilt, aluminum paneled structure for the simple reason that Jaguar expected to sell no more than 200 XK120s in the first year! In conjunction with the Pressed Steel Fisher Company a new all-steel paneled body was developed, which retained the fabulous looks of the coachbuilt original while differing in minor external details. Beneath the skin the steel car considerably different, and it would take some 20 months of development before manufacture could begin.

The XK120's heart was, of course, the fabulous XK engine, developed during the war and intended for Jaguar's forthcoming Mark VII saloon. A 3.4-liter 'six' embodying the best of modern design, it boasted twin overhead camshafts running in an aluminum cylinder head, seven main bearings and a 160bhp rating. The chassis was essentially a shortened version of the simultaneously announced Mark V saloon's, featuring William Heynes's torsion bar independent front suspension. Jaguar lost no time in demonstrating that the XK120's claimed top speed was no idle boast. In May 1949, on the Jabbeke to Aeltre autoroute, an example with its hood and side screens in place recorded speeds of 126mph, and then 132mph with the hood and windscreen detached and an under-tray fitted.

The XK120 set new standards of comfort, roadholding and performance for British sports cars and, in keeping with the Jaguar tradition, there was nothing to touch it at the price. For customers who found the standard car too slow, there was the Special Equipment (SE) package which boosted power to 180bhp. The XK120 was produced until 1954 and would prove to be the most popular of the XK series, with 12,078 examples built, of which 2,194 were left-hand drive SE Roadsters like that offered here.

Factory records show that chassis S675712 was originally finished in Cream over a red interior with a Black soft top. Today, the car is presented in an attractive Dark Blue exterior over a red interior, a color combination believed to have been applied during a comprehensive refurbishment completed approximately a decade ago under previous ownership. The presentation remains faithful to the XK120's elegant proportions and sporting character.

This XK120 retains its original matching-numbers 3,442cc inline-six engine, numbered F3009-8S. The engine number corresponds with both the Jaguar Heritage Certificate and the stamping found on the engine block. In addition, the cylinder head remains matching to the car, further supporting the originality of the drivetrain configuration. Retaining its original engine and matching head configuration, S675712 represents a well-preserved example of Jaguar's iconic early postwar sports car.

TTHE TYPE 35B

"Among racing cars, it is the 1924 Types 35 Bugatti which tops the list of beautiful cars of the (1920s) period. Some would say it's the most beautiful racing car of all time. Although it underwent detail changes through the years and the radiator was enlarged, its lines were virtually unchanged from its appearance in the Grand Prix of the Automobile Club of France in July 1924, through to its final, 51 version of 1931-32." - Autocar magazine.

By the early 1930s Ettore Bugatti had established an unrivalled reputation for building cars with outstanding performance on road or track, the world's greatest racing drivers enjoying countless successes aboard the Molsheim factory's products and often choosing them for their everyday transport. The principal building block of this success was the legendary Type 35, arguably the quintessential Vintage-era sports car, which made its debut in August 1924 at the Grand Prix de l'ACF at Lyon-Givors. The Type 35's 1,991cc straight-eight engine was derived from that of the Type 30 but incorporated five roller/ball main bearings instead of three together with an improved lubrication system. In line with Bugatti's established practice, each cylinder's three valves were actuated by a single overhead camshaft. This state-of-the-art engine went into a conventional chassis with leaf springs at the front and quarter elliptic at the rear, and which boasted a novel hollow front axle and alloy wheels.

The Type 35's debut gave little indication of what was to come, as the factory team of five cars was plagued by tyre troubles and could achieve no better than 7th place at the finish. Despite this debacle the Type 35 in its various forms would go on to become arguably the most successful racing car of all time, commencing with winning the inaugural World Championship for Manufacturers in 1926 and securing countless victories for privateers.

For those who yearn for Bugatti-style motoring yet cannot afford the associated expense, a re-creation is the obvious solution and for many years the classic Type 35 has inspired the construction of numerous examples. Pur Sang of Argentina needs no introduction to those familiar with the world of Bugattis, the firm's Type 35 re-creations being universally admired for their incredible authenticity and quality of execution. This beautiful and highly detailed re-creation represents the model in its ultimate, 2.3-liter supercharged Type 35B form of 1929.

THE BENTLEY AZURE

Based on the potent Bentley Continental R, the drop head Azure version was one of the fastest and most powerful cars of the era. The Geneva Auto Salon was chosen to launch what would turn out to be the first Bentley model in several decades to use an entirely new name – 'Azure' - which, like 'Corniche' and 'Camargue', evoked exotic destinations in the south of France. The famous Italian styling house Pininfarina – a firm with unrivalled experience in the design of soft-top Gran Turismos – had been chosen to develop the Azure on the four-seater Continental R platform, and there was no question that the result was most successful.

Body shells were assembled in Italy by Pininfarina, fitted with the automatic soft-top, painted and shipped to the UK for finishing at the Bentley factory at Crewe. Mechanically the Azure was similar to the Continental R, but with an engine further up-rated to 385bhp. Hailed by its maker as 'the world's best convertible', the Azure lived up to that grand title, proving an immense success especially in the US where its combination of unmatched luxury, effortless performance and soft-top style was highly attractive. When production ceased in 2003, a total of only 1,321 Azures of all types had been built.

THE ALLARD K3

Sydney Allard founded Allard Motor Company in 1936, producing potent sports racing cars powered by Ford V8 and Lincoln V12 engines. Allard racing cars continued to prove themselves as capable competitors, with one example winning the 1952 Monte Carlo Rally piloted by Mr. Allard himself, narrowly defeating Sir Stirling Moss. That same year, Allard released a new touring car based on their venerable J2 racing car, the K3.

Featuring a reinforced chromoly-tube chassis, Allard's innovative divided front axle suspension system, racing steering ratios, and a host of potent American engines, The K3 is a racecar at heart, beneath an all-aluminum envelope body. While the racing attributes limited everyday practicality, the K3 offered undeniable performance along with some welcome luxuries, like seating for three, a spacious trunk, and a convertible top.

The concessions made for performance, along with the steep $5,300 asking price, made the K3's appeal as a touring car suffer. As a result, only 63 of these exhilarating roadsters were produced and just 46 remain today.

THE 1967 FORD BRONCO

Ford introduced the Bronco in August 1965 as a direct response to the growing popularity of compact four-wheel-drive utility vehicles, fielded against the established Jeep CJ-5 and the International Harvester Scout. Designed under the direction of Donald Frey with input from engineer Lew Schuler, the Bronco was engineered from a clean sheet as a purpose-built off-road vehicle rather than a truck-based adaptation, featuring a short 92-inch wheelbase, solid front and rear axles, and available four-wheel drive. Three body styles were offered at launch — a roadster, a half-cab pickup, and a fully enclosed wagon — though the wagon quickly proved the most popular. The half-cab, by contrast, is the rarest and most purposeful of the three body styles: a compact open-bed pickup of distinctly utilitarian character that appealed to those who valued cargo capacity over passenger accommodation. Power in the early years came from Ford's 170 cubic inch inline six as standard, with the larger 200 six and 289 cubic inch V8 available as options. The first-generation Bronco — produced from 1966 through 1977 without significant wheelbase change — is today among the most sought-after American utility vehicles of its era, and the half-cab body style, produced in comparatively small numbers, commands particular interest among collectors.

Often abused more than their Full-Cab siblings, this truck seems to have never hauled anything more than cotton balls and is in fabulous shape.

The truck is reported to have spent many years in Virginia before moving north to Maine, before finally residing in the Greenwich area for some time. The black extended wheel arches appear to be the only departure from the original specification. This presents an opportunity to own a characterful and visually striking early Half-Cab in one of the most appealing color combinations available on the first-generation Bronco. THE PORSCHE 356 SPEEDSTER

The Speedster's inspiration was often credited to John von Neumann, Porsche's West Coast distributor, who had chopped down a Gmünd-built Coupe in the late 1940s to create a lightweight competition car. Explaining such a car's appeal Neumann once said: 'Guys want to go on a Saturday night in June, down Sunset Boulevard with their elbow over the door and the girls can see them in the car.' Plus ça change...

Instantly recognizable by its low, wraparound windscreen, smaller disappearing top, lower door waistline and twin bucket seats, the Speedster was, in effect, an 'economy' model intended to compete with less-expensive British sports cars. While the Speedster concept was von Neumann's, it was East Coast distributor Max Hoffman who convinced Porsche that American buyers would gobble it up. Initially offered with the 1500cc horizontally opposed four, it gained the new 1600, 60bhp engine with the introduction of the improved 356A for 1955.

Priced at $2,995, the Speedster was the lightest of the 356s, enjoying a commensurate performance boost that meant 100mph was possible. With its superb handling, the Speedster became an instant success in the burgeoning American sports car racing scene. Its combination of style, performance and value for money made the Speedster deservedly popular. Today the model enjoys iconic status and is cherished by collectors.


THE CAR OFFERED

Chassis number 83066 carries a history traceable to its very first sale: the Kardex on file confirms delivery through Hoffman Motors of New York on March 12, 1957, the storied Manhattan dealership that served as Porsche's principal East Coast representative during the marque's formative years in America. A letter on Porsche letterhead, signed by Jürgen Barth and dated September 19, 1975, further corroborates the factory colors – rot (red) over black leatherette, lending the car an uncommon degree of early documentation. The original windscreen includes parking stickers from Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois from 1966 and '67.

Spending the vast majority of its life in the Midwest, it was acquired by the present seller in Chicago in August 2013 following extended storage in Missouri, the car subsequently underwent a thorough refurbishment spanning December 2016 to April 2023. Bodywork was entrusted to The Tin Man's Garage of Sycamore, Illinois, where the shell was stripped to bare metal, revealing that the car had left the factory in red. Structural repairs addressed prior rear-end damage of apparent track origin and encompassed replacement of the rear clip, passenger door skin, floors, and battery box. A two-stage repaint in black was executed by Posematos's Bodyworks and Restorations of Gurnee, Illinois.

While the original engine, no. 64715, is no longer with the car, correct-type motor now sits in the engine bay. The replacement Type 616/1 flat-four, no. 62349, was rebuilt and enlarged to 1,720cc, fitted with Wilhoit Auto Restoration cylinder heads, JE forged pistons, a DPR 74mm counterweighted crankshaft, and an LN Engineering camshaft. Induction is by dual Solex PBIC carburetors with Knecht air filters. The four-speed manual transaxle was rebuilt by 356 Works of Glenview, Illinois, in February 2016, while the drum brakes — overhauled by J&G Brake Drum Relining & Refinishing of McHenry, Illinois, in March 2020 — are equipped with Koni dampers at all four corners. A YnZ's wiring harness was installed in 2021.

The re-chromed ventilated steel wheels are shod with 165VR15 Pirelli Cinturato CN36 tires, with a matching spare carried in the front boot. The tan leatherette interior — sourced from Autos International of Escondido, California, and fitted in 2021 — extends across the fixed-back bucket seats, rear bench, dashboard, and door panels, complemented by oatmeal square-weave carpeting and matching Coco mats. Green-letter VDO instrumentation -- restored by Palo Alto Speedometer -- includes a central tachometer, 120mph speedometer, and combination oil temperature and pressure gauge. In August 2025, the steering wheel rim, dash knobs, and door release trim were refinished in tan. The five-digit odometer reads just under 93,012 miles at the time of cataloging; the seller advises that 320 miles have been added since completion of the refurbishment.

Offered with a Kardex copy, the 1975 Barth letter, refurbishment photographs and records, a replica tool kit sourced from Harvey Rosenthal, the original windshield glass — bearing 1966 and 1967 Northwestern University parking decals, side curtains, half tonneau cover, and a car cover, this Speedster is ready for its next owner.

THE PORSCHE 944 TURBO

The idea of evolution rather than revolution, is a mantra that Porsche enthusiasts know all too well. When Porsche introduced their joint-venture 924 in 1976, the machine received positive reviews from critics but was criticized by Porsche enthusiasts for its Audi derived 2-liter engine. Porsche released a widely improved Turbo variant (Type 931), but it carried a higher cost and garnered poor sales. Rather than scrap the design, Porsche developed the Type 944 in 1982, following uniformly from generations of 911s before it.

The re-worked platform carried an inline 2.5 Liter 4-Cylinder, effectively half of the 928's 5.0 V8, while the revised bodywork showcased aesthetic changes similar to that of the 924 Carrera GT. 1986 saw the addition of a turbocharger and intercooler and a new model internally referred to as the Type 951. Power increased more than 50% over standard naturally aspirated cars thanks to the KKK turbocharger, producing 217 horsepower and 243lb ft of torque. In keeping with Porsche's characteristic engineering philosophy, the engine was mounted well behind the front axle and its gearbox positioned at the rear as a transaxle, achieving a weight distribution close to equal. In addition to the engine work, the bodywork was widened to accommodate broader tracks front and rear, the suspension was recalibrated to manage the considerable increase in performance, and the braking system was upgraded to four-piston calipers at each corner. The result was a car that could accelerate from rest to 60mph in under six seconds and reach a top speed approaching 160mph, while remaining tractable and rewarding in everyday use.

The 944 Turbo is one of the most naturally balanced performance cars of its era. Automotive journalists of the period were almost unanimous in their praise, and the passage of time has only strengthened the 951's reputation as one of the most accomplished driver's cars to emerge from Zuffenhausen in the 1980s.

An exciting opportunity for any enthusiast to own a "real" Porsche, ready for whatever summer adventures its new caretaker has in store.

Overseas sales have always been important to Harley-Davidson, which explains the 350cc singles that debuted in 1926. Riders in Great Britain, Europe and Australia, goaded by increased road taxes on larger-capacity machines, were the prime audience, as were fans of lightweight, maneuverable bikes here in the U.S. It also helped that the AMA had just instituted a 21-inch racing division for 350-class machines. For racers or those who wanted spirited road bikes, 12-horsepower overhead-valve 350s were available in limited numbers. These quickly gained the "Peashooter" nickname for their popping exhaust note. Most of the bikes, though, like this nicely restored B-model, ran 8-hp sidevalve-design engines, the B in this case representing battery ignition as opposed to the magneto-equipped A-models.

This particular Harley was part of the collection of Norman Hobday. A Bay Area character, he was known as Henry Africa and operated a number of local watering holes. An astute collector of vintage motorcycles and Tiffany lamps, this bike hung for decades above the bar at his San Francisco bar, Capt. Eddie Rickenbacker's, in SOMA below which countless Irish Coffees were no doubt consumed (including by this cataloger). After his passing in 2011, the motorcycle was sold at Bonhams's 2012 Quail Lodge Sale and entered the collection of the current keeper.

On long term static display since acquisition, it has been decades since this Harley was last actively ridden. Ready for a recommissioning, it will no doubt put a smile on the face of the next owner – whether they are riding it or having a cocktail underneath it.

THE 1950 MERCURY CONVERTIBLE

Few automobiles in American history have proven as fertile a canvas for the custom car builder as the 1949–1951 Mercury: low, long, and possessed of a slab-sided simplicity that rewarded modification. The "ShoeboxMercury" — as the styling idiom of the era came to be known — became the defining subject of the postwar custom movement almost from the moment it appeared. The lead sculptors of the era, among them Sam and George Barris, Gene Winfield, and Larry Watson, returned to the Mercury body repeatedly throughout the 1950s, and the car's profile became so synonymous with the Kustom Kulture movement that it remains its most iconic representative today. The standard powertrain — a flathead V8 of Mercury specification — was frequently replaced by later overhead-valve units offering greater output, while the body itself invited every manner of modification: chopped tops, extended decks, frenched headlights and taillights, removed door handles, and radical paintwork among them. The result, at its best, was an object of genuine sculptural ambition — a popular automobile transformed into something approaching automotive folk art.

THE PORSCHE 356

Porsche's Type 356, introduced in 1948, is acknowledged to be one of the world's great sports cars. Over a 15-year production run, the handsome and durable 356 evolved from a streamlined little aluminum-bodied coupe powered by a VW-derived, 46bhp 1100cc air-cooled flat four to a powerful autobahn burner carrying a complex, two-liter four-cam boxer Carrera engine, producing 130bhp. The cars steady development brought not only coupes, but introduced luxurious cabriolets, speedsters, and roadsters. In all there were more than 76,000 examples built by the time production ceased in 1965.

The 356B, produced from 1960 through 1963, represents the mid-point in this design's progression. In what is known as "T5" form, the B introduced new front and rear sheet-metal, while retaining the curved front trunk lid and rounded fenders of the 356A series. The B also added some features demanded by American customers, such as raised front and rear bumpers with over-riders to better protect the body from parking mishaps. The headlamps were raised, a larger hood handle added, and front vent windows appeared in the doors. Mechanically, the gearbox and drum brakes were upgraded. A new steering wheel and column refreshed the interior, along with redesigned rear seats. A "Super" model with raised compression added an extra 15bhp over the standard version, while the even hotter Super 90 added 30bhp – a full 50% more power than the base car.

The 356 made its final transformation with the Type 6 body in 1963. Designated 356C, it had a new ZF steering gear and added compensating springs at the rear, the latter calming the swing axle suspension. Four-wheel disc brakes were also part of the revision, and a 12-volt electrical system became available. Two 1,600 cc engines were offered, the "C" version with 75DIN (European horsepower, rated 88 by SAE), and the "SC" with higher compression and counterweighted crankshaft making 95DIN (107 SAE).

This Porsche was delivered new through AFN Ltd. in England around April of 1961. The Kardex further lists the car returned for service a few times with the last record dated November 8, 1961, with about 9,144km on the odometer.

Appearing to be very well-kept, it has been the recipient of an older, complete restoration, still presenting very well today. The previous long-term owner of this Super 90 Cabriolet was a huge Porsche enthusiast and ensured his Porsche was a great example to begin with and received a full restoration completed to a high standard. Mechanically, the well-detailed Super 90 motor is the same powerplant the car was born with, requisite with the impressive 90 horsepower this car deserved.

This Porsche will be accompanied with a copy of its Kardex report, Porsche Certificate of Authenticity, Porsche driver's manual, document file, tool kit and jack. A popular car for tours and rallies such as the Copperstate 1000, Going to the Sun, and New England 1000, this Super 90 Cabriolet is sure to provide plenty of top-down fun and smiles.

Hudson was among the first of the Detroit automakers to introduce new models after World War II, and they were without question the most dramatically different of all the new designs.

Hudson's innovation for 1948 was the "step-down" chassis with the foot wells recessed between the body stiffening members, an early expression of the "unit body" concept, which merged the body and frame in a single, welded unit. The rear frame members passed outside the rear wheels: the Hudson's rear wheel skirts were functional, not pointless embellishment. The first "step-down" Hudson's were only five feet high. They were the fastest, best handling cars around, combining Hudson's competent six- and eight-cylinder engines with the low center of gravity and relatively lightweight of the "step-down" design.

The Detroit-based company celebrated its 40th anniversary in 1949 with a line of cars that continued the popular "step-down" design introduced the year before. Even as other American automakers caught up with their first fully redesigned post-WWII cars, the 1949 Hudson enjoyed a 36-percent gain in sales from 1948.

The underdog Hudson entered racing in 1951. Success was easily found in NASCAR with the bigger, straight eight Hornet. The Hudson's superiority on oval tracks was no fluke, either. In the 195 2 Mexican Road Race Marshall Teague brought his Hudson Wasp home sixth overall. On some of the twisting, broken surfaced sections through the Mexican mountains he blew off all the entries from sports car powers Porsche, Lancia and Jaguar.

Nevertheless, unable to introduce new models as fast as its larger rivals, and lacking a V8 engine, Hudson was forced to merge with Nash in 1954, forming American Motors.

MERCEDES-BENZ 280 SE 3.5 CABRIOLET

In the pantheon of postwar luxury automobiles, few models command the reverence, and admiration accorded the Mercedes-Benz W111-series Cabriolet, and none more so than the potent and lavishly appointed 280 SE 3.5. Introduced in late 1969, the 3.5-liter variant marked the ultimate evolution of the prestigious W111 platform, at once marrying Mercedes-Benz's storied engineering prowess with newfound V8 performance and subtle, old-world elegance.

Conceived at a time when Mercedes-Benz sought to reaffirm its leadership within the realm of open Grand Tourers, the 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet combined the sweeping, pillarless silhouette of the original Paul Bracq-penned design with significant mechanical advancements. At its heart lay the M116 V8: a single-overhead-cam, all-alloy motor of 3,499 cubic centimeters, breathing through sophisticated Bosch D-Jetronic electronic fuel injection. This combination yielded an exhilarating 200bhp, a figure that transformed the W111 Cabriolet from stately tourer to swift express, fully capable of sustained Autobahn velocities.

Hand-assembled in limited numbers at the legendary Sindelfingen works, the 3.5 Cabriolet was a singular accomplishment, blending robust German engineering with the finest materials available. The opulent interiors featured exotic wood veneers, hand-stitched leather, and finely chromed hardware—details emblematic of Mercedes-Benz's uncompromising standard of craftsmanship. Furthermore, the model's fully independent suspension and four-wheel disc brakes complemented the powerful V8, ensuring dynamic poise and refined composure on both sweeping highways and sinuous country roads.

The exclusivity of the 3.5 Cabriolet was defined not only by its performance or luxury, but also by its scarcity. Just 1,232 Cabriolets were produced between 1969 and 1971, and fewer still were delivered to original European specification. Today, their desirability persists, with discerning collectors coveting unrestored examples or those returned to as-new condition by the world's foremost specialists.

The 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet enjoys an exalted reputation amongst Mercedes-Benz connoisseurs, owing to its place as the final hand-built, open-top model of the classic era. It stands as Mercedes-Benz's swan song to a world before mass production altered the automotive landscape—a graceful, V8-powered masterwork embodying both the manufacturer's technical acumen and its dedication to understated elegance.

In period, the 3.5 Cabriolet was the preferred conveyance of captains of industry, film stars, and heads of state, offering unparalleled comfort and performance in equal measure. Its effortless road manners, ample power reserves, and whisper-quiet operation set a benchmark that rivals and successors would struggle to attain.

Further elevating its appeal is the car's ability to blend discreet luxury with subtle aggression. At a glance, the casual observer might miss the discreet "3.5" badging and low, wide grille—further emphasizing its status as a sophisticated grand tourer for those who value substance over ostentation.

Today, the W111 280 SE 3.5 Cabriolet stands at the zenith of postwar Mercedes-Benz collector interest, cherished for its rarity, integrity, and fully realized synthesis of performance and grace. The finest examples—those retaining their original mechanicals and finished in compelling color schemes—are considered blue-chip investments within the international collector community.

THE FERRARI 308

In the early 1970s, Ferrari was known for its powerful V12 engines that dominated both the racetrack and the road. Enzo Ferrari had long resisted the idea of producing road cars with fewer than twelve cylinders. But the company needed a more accessible, affordable entry point to the fabled brand, and that compromise had already begun with the Dino sub-brand — a V6-engined car sold without the Ferrari badge.

When production of the Dino 246 was discontinued in mid-1974, the only junior Ferrari available was the recently introduced 308 GT4. However, the GT4's 2+2 cockpit layout and controversial Bertone styling divided opinion. Ferrari needed a pure two-seater that could carry the prancing horse badge with pride — and returned to Pininfarina to build it.

The new entry-level model caused a stir when it debuted at the Paris Motor Show in 1975 — it was the first mid-engined V8 ever to wear the Ferrari badge. The long-awaited replacement for the Dino 246 GT had a pronounced wedge profile, with a rectangular egg-crate aluminum radiator grille below a slim full-width satin black bumper. However, numerous key design elements of the Dino 246 GT were carried through — the scalloped door intakes, twin circular rear light assemblies, and the vertical concave rear screen bounded by buttressed sail panels.

The GTB was the first Ferrari to benefit from being developed in Pininfarina's wind tunnel. The result was 0–60 mph in around 6.5 seconds and a top speed of over 150 mph. The first models boasted fiberglass coachwork — the first Ferrari production car to feature this body material. This kept weight to just 1,050 kg, making the early cars the lightest and most driver-focused of all 308's.

Despite having fewer than Enzo's requisite 12 cylinders, the 308 GTB was badged and marketed as a Ferrari — a victory for the money men at parent company Fiat, no doubt, but one warmly embraced by customers. It looked terrific, had excellent performance, and cost barely two-thirds of the price of a Berlinetta Boxer.

By mid-1977, a return to more traditional pressed steel and aluminum bodywork happened — for USA cars in late 1976 and European models around mid-1977. The switch added roughly 150 kg but improved build quality and paint consistency.

More significantly, Ferrari launched a targa-top version of the 308 GTB known as the 308 GTS at the Frankfurt Motor Show in 1977. Visually it was very similar to the GTB apart from the black finished solid removable glass-fiber roof panel and the satin black finished hinged opening louvre panels over the rear quarter windows. The chassis was reinforced in key places to compensate for the lack of a full roof rigidity. The GTS would go on to vastly outsell the closed GTB for the rest of the car's life.

When Ferrari had to reduce the car's emissions in 1980, it switched from carburetors to a Bosch K-Jetronic fuel-injection system — and the result was a loss of about 55 PS. US-market cars suffered the most, fitted with catalytic converters that pushed output below 200 hp. These "i" models — the GTBi and GTSi — are the least celebrated of the 308 family, though they kept the showroom busy while Ferrari worked on a solution.

The Ferrari 308 was made famous by the television series Magnum, P.I., in which the series' lead Thomas Magnum (Tom Selleck) drove the car around Oahu for eight seasons while on his investigations, from 1980 to 1988. Several 308 GTS cars were used — a new one for each season, mostly being auctioned off after filming, all with the license plate "ROBIN 1".

The iconic pairing almost never happened. Selleck initially pushed for his character to drive a Porsche 928, but the automaker declined production modifications. Ferrari stepped in, customizing the 308 GTS to fit Selleck's 6-foot-4 frame by adjusting the seat height and positioning.

For eight years, Selleck drove his red sidekick through 162 episodes, ensuring that the Prancing Horse was top of mind everywhere from New York penthouses to double-wide mobile homes across America. Ferrari's American sales surged, and the 308 became arguably the most recognized sports car of the decade.

In 1982, Ferrari introduced four-valve technology into the 308 lineup, resulting in the Quattrovalvole versions of both the coupe and the targa. One other significant benefit of the QV's four-valve heads was the replacement of the non-QV models' sodium valves, which had been known to fail at the joint between the head and the stem. European cars now made 240bhp, and the car felt properly fast again.

The QV era also spawned a motorsport legend. From the workshops at Michelotto in Padua, a Group 4 rally car was developed, with the first model leaving in 1978. Its first victory came in 1979 at the Monza Rally. By 1982, the 308 Gr4 won both the constructors' and drivers' titles of the Italian Rally Championship.

By the time the 308 was finally replaced, 12,149 examples of both the Berlinetta and open-top spider models had left the line — making it the best-selling Ferrari in history at that point.

Identified by its 'M' VIN prefix, this is a confirmed US-specification Quattrovalvole, factory-built to meet American emissions requirements and fitted with catalytic converters. Its sequential chassis number places it squarely in the middle of the 1983 production run, built at a time when demand in North America was at its peak, fueled in no small part by the car's starring role in Magnum, P.I.


The GTS body — penned by Leonardo Fioravanti at Pininfarina and built by Scaglietti — features the model's distinctive removable black roof panel, louvred rear quarter windows, four-outlet exhaust, and quad taillights with reversing lamps on the outer pair; detail changes that visually separate the QV from its predecessors.

Finished in traditional Rosso Corsa over Beige leather sport seats, the interior consists of the gated manual transmission, and a period correct Alpine AM/FM CD player.

Accompanying the car are multiple keys, original tool roll and jack, along with its targa roof panel.

Showing just 51,286 miles at the time of cataloging, live out your Magnum P.I. fantasies.

Of the 3,042 GTS Quattrovalvole examples built between 1982 and 1985, US-specification 1983 cars represent a single, narrow production window — all sharing the 'M' engine code unique to that model year and market.

THE 996 TURBO CABRIOLET

The Porsche 911 Turbo occupies a singular position among world-class sports cars, fusing inspirational engineering, open-air motoring, and superlative, daily-drivable performance in a way few rivals have achieved. Long an icon of well-heeled enthusiasts, the 911 Turbo legend grew ever more formidable with the arrival of the Type 996 Turbo in 2000. As the first modern, water-cooled 911 Turbo, its formidable twin-turbocharged flat-six powerplant, derived from the storied 911 GT1 Le Mans winner, brought a new threshold of power and composure to the Stuttgart marque.

In 2004, Porsche raised the stakes, introducing the Turbo Cabriolet variant—delivering all-weather, all-roof-down capability in an astonishingly rapid, highly refined package. The recipe instantly became a 21st-century masterstroke: the security and confidence of all-wheel drive, overwhelming acceleration from near-idle speeds thanks to twin KKK turbochargers, and the sonic thrill of 415 horsepower funneled through Porsche's precise 6-speed manual. In typical Teutonic fashion, the transformation was executed with no compromise to performance or chassis rigidity, the cabriolet's architecture boasting sophisticated reinforcements for open-top use.

Complemented by sophisticated active aerodynamics—including a hydraulically deployed rear spoiler—and Porsche's cutting-edge Ceramic Composite Brakes, the 996 Turbo Cabriolet set benchmarks in both speed and control. These brake discs, boasting lower unsprung weight and near fade-proof operation, remain a high watermark of engineering, emblematic of Porsche's relentless pursuit of performance without compromise.

Rare optionality's like the coveted Turbo Power Kit delivered a tangible surge in performance, further pushing the envelope of what the "everyday supercar" could accomplish. Superbly balanced, with confidence-inspiring traction, and engineered for grand touring or spirited drives alike, the 911 Turbo Cabriolet succeeded in democratizing world-class speed with everyday usability—and doing so with arresting style.

Now legitimately considered modern classics, 996-era Porsche Turbos are increasingly sought after for their purity of feel, analog interface, and distinctive design. The Cabriolet, produced in far lesser numbers than its coupe stablemate, elevates that rarity, offering discerning collectors a true confluence of significance, specification, and open-air exhilaration.

Presenting today with its factory livery and a careful history of enthusiast stewardship, this example is emblematic of the breed: a rolling testament to Porsche's relentless drive toward perfection, executed at the highest level for both connoisseur and driver. As Type 996 Turbos continue their upward trajectory in collector esteem, cabriolet examples in preserved, well-documented condition stand among the most desirable.

THE SUPER SIX

Introduced as a lower-priced companion to the parent Hudson marque in 1919, the Essex soon became synonymous with both high performance and reliability when an example averaged over 60mph for 50 hours in December 1919, a stunt which the company followed up by a successful four-car transcontinental trek in 1920.

Founded in Detroit, Michigan in 1910, the Hudson Motor Car Company took its name from Joseph L. Hudson, who provided the finances that enabled a group of experienced ex-Olds Motor Works employees to embark on a new automobile manufacturing venture. Incorporated in February 1909, Hudson built its first car in July of that same year and 12 months later had sold 4,000 units, the industry's best first-year sales record to date. Although the firm would later become famous for its record-breaking Super Six range, Hudson's first product was a four-cylinder car, as was that of companion marque Essex.

Essex pioneered low-cost closed coachwork in the United States, its four-seater sedan being only slightly more expensive than the tourer in 1922 and marginally cheaper by 1925. Essex's big news for 1924 was the switch from four to six cylinders. The new sidevalve power unit started life at an unusually small - for the United States - 2.1 liters capacity before being enlarged to 2.4 liters part way through the year. Renamed 'Super Six' for 1927, the Essex gained a larger and more powerful engine that year and four-wheel Bendix mechanical brakes the year after. Stylistically, the Essex looked broadly similar to its Hudson parent, albeit on a smaller scale.

Of the Essex lineup in 1927 the most exciting model available was unquestionable the Speedabout. A boattailed roadster body with a leather trimmed cockpit by Amesbury, Massachusetts coachbuilder Biddle & Smart—which bodied many of more limited-production bodies—it was sleek and fast thanks to a special gear set found only in this model that gave it 80mph performance. Its strong curb appeal helped get buyers into the showroom—more often to buy one of Essex's more practical, and expensive, models. It is unknown exactly how many Speedabout were made, but the numbers were slim and today only about a dozen still exist.

This Speedabout is finished in fire engine red over black upholstery and looks to be a tidy restoration that has settled into a fine driver quality machine over the past few decades. Rolling on artillery style wheels that are color matched to the car and accented with black pinstripes, the sporty machine is simply trimmed inside and offset nicely with a steering wheel fashioned from polished wood.

Throw a Ben Pollack record on the player, put on your three piece and hit the road in style.

"The Giulietta Spider must have been quite a shock to the other manufacturers of small sports cars when it was first released to the public. Suddenly, there was a new state of the art. With its roll-up windows, excellent ride and delightfully simple top mechanism, the Spider made all the other sporting vehicles of 1955 look terribly dated." - Joe Benson, Alfa Romeo Buyer's Guide.

With the introduction of the Giulietta, Alfa Romeo established the 'small car, big performance' formula that would characterize the Milanese marque's finest offerings from then on. First of the Giuliettas, the Bertone-styled Giulietta Sprint Coupé debuted at the Turin Motor Show in April 1954, powered by a 1.3-liter, all-alloy version of Alfa's classic twin-cam four designed by one-time Ferrari engineer Giuseppe Busso. Without equal at the time, this wonderful engine produced 80bhp in the regular Spider and 90 horsepower in the Veloce version that followed.

The original 750-Series Giulietta Sprint Coupé of 1954 was soon joined by Berlina and Spider versions. Designed and built by Pininfarina and notable as the famous Turin coachbuilder's first volume-produced car, the Spider brought a level of refinement and mechanical sophistication to small sports cars that made the opposition look dated. The combination of a rev-happy engine, fine-handling, responsive chassis and excellent brakes make these Giuliettas a driver's car par excellence and explains why these stylish Alfa Romeos continue to attract the discerning enthusiast today.

From Milwaukee, the good land, comes the great bike, the iconic V-Rod was Harley Davidson's first break from its long-standing tradition of air-cooled V-twins. When introduced, it was the most sporting offering Harley had offered in years and included numerous innovations. Updated over its 16 year's production run, it stands today as one of Harley's most iconic recent models.

No other model showed just how far Harley-Davidson had come from its founding in 1903 than the 100th Anniversary V-Rod. The bike's 1130cc "Revolution" V twin, introduced the year before, developed from the company's AMA Superbike program with a helping hand from Porsche engineering, was the first Harley powerplant to feature liquid cooling and overhead camshafts. It delivered 115hp, far more than any stock; streetable Harley-Davidson had ever produced. With its all-silver livery it is in retrospect a much more futuristic style forward machine then was appreciated at the time. None the less the motoring press loved the new offering from the Milwaukee firm. "Harley didn't just think outside the box, it blew the box away!" said Motorcycle Cruiser magazine at the time of the bike's debut. "The V-Rod certainly doesn't fall anywhere near the various niches Harley has created previously, and it forces us to expand our thinking about what a Harley can be technologically, aesthetically and functionally."

Realizing this bike's significance, the original owner purchased it as a collector's item, always stored it indoors, and it appears as new today as it would have in your local Harley Davidson Dealer in 2003. This example has recorded, a scarcely believable 16 miles (at the time of cataloging) since it rolled off the production line. Back in 1953, Chevrolet's launch of a two-seater sports car was a radical departure for a marque hitherto associated almost exclusively with sensible family transport. Based on the 1952 EX-122 show car, the Corvette made use of existing GM running gear and a shortened chassis frame, around which was wrapped striking Harley Earl-styled fiberglass coachwork. Motive power came from Chevrolet's 235 cubic inch overhead-valve straight six and, unusually for a sports car, there was automatic transmission, a feature that attracted much adverse criticism at the time. Intended as competition for the T-Series MG, the Corvette cost way above the target figure, ending up in Jaguar XK120 territory but with an inferior performance. Sales were sluggish initially and the model came close to being axed, surviving thanks to Chevrolet's need to compete with Ford's Thunderbird. A V8 engine for 1955 and a radical restyle for '56 consolidated the 'Vette's position in the market.

Chevrolet's introduction of the option of fuel injection for the 1957 season was inspired for it provided the now bored out 283 cubic inch V8 with a matched number of horses under the hood. It was first tested as a solution to gas 'sloshing' of carburetor aspirated cars turning into bends under race conditions at Sebring in 1956 and then rolled out as an option for the next production season. Retrospectively it is amazing to think that Chevrolet was able to offer this contemporaneously with Mercedes-Benz's 300SL, while on other high-end machinery it would be more than a decade before this would be the commonplace. And all at once, the term 'fuelie' was born.

By this time, Corvettes had begun to establish an enviable competition record for the marque. Corvette Chief Engineer Zora Arkus-Duntov was a big fan of auto racing, and it was he that was responsible for unlocking the car's innate potential and development it into a genuine race-winner. These racing successes repaid Chevrolet's investment with interest: Corvette sales improved significantly, ensuring the car's survival and enabling it to go on to become the world's best-selling and longest-lived sports car. In 1957, 6,339 Corvettes were produced, but only 714 were ordered with the RPO (Regular Production Order) 579B option box ticked for the $484.20 Ramjet fuel injected V8 that delivered one horsepower for every cubic inch of engine capacity. It's little wonder so few were ordered given that a base Corvette retailed for $3,176.32.


THE CAR OFFERED

Offered here is a spectacular example of the classic 1957 Corvette. This 283 Chevy V8 is mated to the sports-oriented 4-speed manual transmission. While this Corvette wears Fuel Injection badges on its fenders, the car is currently equipped with an Edelbrock 4-barrel carburetor. The restoration on the car is of an indeterminate age but is presenting quite well. The convertible top is in wonderful shape and includes the "dealer do not remove" tag. The interior is redone but of factory type materials. Overall, this Corvette is a sharp and classic slice of americana and would be welcome at nearly any event, and fully capable of the "Ice Cream Run". The car has been sitting for a period of time but runs at the time of cataloging.

THE FABCAR

Fabcar is an American racing design and fabrication shop founded by Dave Klym in 1977, located in Tucker, Georgia. They specialize in designing and constructing high-performance race cars, particularly for endurance racing and sports car competitions, and are known for meticulous craftsmanship and cutting-edge technology.

The first outlines of Fabcar began in the late 1970s through the hands of Dave Klym, a talented mechanic from Carmel, Indiana, who was already a well-known face on and off tracks across the USA — both as an amateur GT racing driver and as a mechanic, having worked for teams including Dan Gurney's All American Racing and Charlie Hayes Racing.

Fabcar's first major project was building eleven-Wheeler Super V cars. In 1979, Fabcar was contracted to build three Lightning Indy cars for Lindsay Hopkins from Atlanta — among the first ground-effect Indy cars, designed by David Bruns, who later went on to start Swift Cars.

One of Fabcar's most notable achievements is the development of the Fabcar Porsche 935, a dominant force in IMSA racing during the 1980s.

In the 1980s, Fabcar built customer Porsche 962s and 935s in the same tradition as Kremer or Joest in Europe, becoming a worldwide expert on the Porsche chassis design.

The most extreme example was the JLP-4, built for JLP Racing (John Paul Sr. & Jr.). The JLP Racing team wanted to build a version of the 935 that could "win any race it entered" with no expense spared. The car's 3,200 cc engine was reportedly capable of around 840 hp at 20.5 psi of boost. It featured a prototype-style slab-sided centre section with sliding skirts that sealed the underbody aerodynamics, and switchable diffuser stalling flaps to increase top speed on the straights — by far the most sophisticated and aerodynamically advanced Porsche 911-based racing car of its time.

The Porsche 935/84 is another significant Fabcar creation. This car was originally constructed for Bob Akin Motor Racing and participated in the 1982 IMSA GT Championship as a Porsche 935 L-1. A broken axle during qualifying led to a crash with Derek Bell at the wheel, and the car was sent to Dave Klym at Fabcar in Tucker, Georgia. The chassis was rebuilt and christened the 935/84 before debuting at the Daytona Finale Three Hours in November 1983, achieving a second-place finish. It was driven by Patrick Long at Rennsport Reunion V in 2015.

The most audacious Fabcar creation was a mid-engined Porsche 993 — flipping the entire layout of the air-cooled 911 platform. The unique 993 ME demonstrated all of Fabcar's boldness and determination in its pursuit of innovation in motorsport and remains one of its most celebrated creations.

Fabcar's expertise spans chassis fabrication, aerodynamic optimization, and advanced suspension systems. Revered as one of the most important companies in the Porsche segment in the 1980s and 1990s, Fabcar left an impressive legacy on the racetrack, with its products synonymous with reliability, novelty, and speed. Their cars remain highly sought after in the historic racing world — Fabcar's rarely come up for sale.


THE CAR OFFERED

Commissioned in the early 1990s with an open budget, Chassis no. 119210281 is one of the most purposeful and historically significant Porsche-based competition cars built in America. The chromoly tube-frame chassis was designed and fabricated by Dave Klym of Klym Engineering — the man behind Fabcar — whose work defined American Porsche endurance racing throughout the 1980s and 1990s. The A.I.R. 993 fiberglass bodywork, early 911 steel roof section, and Type 964 race engine and transaxle were built and fitted by Paul Willison of Willison Werkstat in Florida. Upon completion in the mid-1990s, noted IMSA driver JLP Jr. was engaged for final setup and shakedown. The build cost reportedly exceeded $250,000 — the equivalent of well over half a million dollars at today's value.

Tragically, the original owner suffered a stroke shortly after the car's completion and it was never campaigned as intended. It remained in Willison's Florida shop for approximately seven years before being acquired in 2002 by William Eaddy, who at that time also owned a 1967 911R, a 1973 2.8 RSR, a 1994 3.8 RSR, and a 996 GT3 Cup car. Eaddy raced the Fabcar twelve times between 2002 and 2015, predominantly in SCCA GT-2 at Palm Beach International Raceway, securing eight first-place finishes. He later described it as the best-handling Porsche he had ever driven in, including his 996 GT3 Cup car.

In 2015 the car passed to IMSA Driver of the Year Jack Lewis, who further developed it for GT-2 competition. Lewis raced it six times in the SCCA Majors Tour. Notably, his wife Helga — racing in her 70s — took a third-place finish at VIR on her first outing. Lewis himself secured two Majors victories and finished second overall in GT-2 P2 class points for the season.

The heart of the car is a PMNA high-compression 3.6-liter Type 964 flat-six race engine, fully rebuilt and producing in excess of 350 bhp on pump fuel. Induction is handled by a set of rebuilt and re-jetted PMO 50mm carburetors — among the finest aftermarket carburetors available for any air-cooled Porsche engine — paired with a period Electromotive ignition system. Drive is taken through a right-side-up 934 4-speed close-ratio racing transaxle sourced from Bob Akin Racing in 1977, fitted with a new Guard Transmission Pro Series limited-slip differential.

The Fabcar chromoly tube-frame chassis is in excellent condition and is notably lighter, stronger, and more rigid than any steel unibody equivalent. Suspension is fully adjustable RSR coil-over specification with restored Koni dampers and 930 trailing arms, engineered by Fabcar with their characteristic approach to camber adjustment — visible in the photographs. Braking is provided by Porsche 993 Turbo 'Big Red' calipers at the front and adapted 917 front calipers at the rear, with cabin-adjustable front-to-rear bias.

The restored fiberglass body and steel roof section are finished in iconic Gulf Racing Blue and carry the car's original racing number, 59. Glazing throughout uses lightweight custom-fabricated aluminum frames with Lexan — designed to be removed quickly for open-air driving. Three NACA ducts provide ventilation to the cabin and engine bay. The rear quarter windows open in the manner of an early 911 and double as engine air feeds.

Despite its competition specification, the car has been thoughtfully prepared for dual-purpose use. Electric air conditioning and cabin heat — the latter drawn ingeniously from one of the three front-mounted engine oil coolers — were added at a combined weight penalty of just 30 lbs., positioned behind the front axle, fitting perfectly within the chassis. Lightweight sound deadening lines the engine and transaxle firewall, concealed beneath matte German leather-trimmed luan panels. Height-adjustable Porsche 993 seats provide comfort on road events, with the option to substitute the included MOMO FIA race seat, reducing overall curb weight to 2,125 lbs. with a full fuel cell.

Wheels are the original 16-inch BBS magnesium racing items — 11.0 x 16 front, 12.5 x 16 rear — in fine original condition.

The car underwent a comprehensive two-year restoration by The R Institute, completed in 2026. Since restoration it has been driven only on test drives and to one local show. It has never been involved in an accident, carries relatively low chassis hours, and presents in great mechanical and cosmetic condition throughout.

Accompanying the car are the original logbook, build records/photos/documentation, restoration records, owner instructions, new MOMO FIA seat, race net and race belts.

This documented Fabcar chassis is street-registered and eligible for La Carrera Panamericana, Porsche Club of America events, SCCA racing, Historic Racing with HSR and SVRA, Pikes Peak Hillclimb, and Driver's Education events. With its electric air conditioning and road registration, it is equally at home on a rally stage, at Cars and Coffee, or on track.

THE 1978 CHEVROLET CORVETTE

The 1978 Corvette marked the model's 25th anniversary and arrived as the most significantly updated Shark-body car since the generation's 1968 introduction, distinguished by a new fastback roofline with a large wraparound rear window that transformed both the silhouette and interior light. Power is provided by the 350 cubic inch small-block V8, available in standard L48 or high-output L82 tune, driving through either a four-speed manual or three-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic automatic transmission. The anniversary year also brought a special two-tone Silver Anniversary paint option and, for pace car replicas, the striking black-over-silver livery commemorating the model's selection as Indianapolis 500 pace car — the second time a Corvette had been so honored. With 46,776 produced, the 1978 remains among the more accessible entry points into classic Corvette ownership, combining the visceral character of the Shark body with a level of interior refinement and equipment that earlier cars in the series could not match.

It remains in its original, unaltered condition, retaining the authentic features and components that make it a true collector's item.

THE BMW ISETTA

Popular during the 1950s and 1960s, the diminutive 'bubble car' or 'cabin scooter' is currently enjoying a revival of interest - not surprisingly given the congested state of today's urban roads. Nowadays though, the Bubble's attraction has just as much to do with fashion as practicality. One of the more successful designs of the cabin scooter's heyday was the BMW Isetta, a design the German firm manufactured under license from its Italian originator Iso. The name means 'little Iso'. Renzo Rivoltas Iso was not selling well in its native Italy, faced with stiff competition from the FIAT 500 and 600, and it would be left to BMW to fully exploit the design's potential.

Although at first glance a three-wheeler, the German-built Isetta used a pair of closely spaced wheels at the rear and was powered by a BMW single-cylinder four-stroke motorcycle engine of 247cc, replacing the original's noisy two-stroke motor. The coachwork of early examples featured a side-hinged single door at the front, roll-top sunroof, and fixed side windows, while the steering wheel and dashboard were attached to the door to facilitate entry. The two-seater Isettas most popular accessory, understandably so given the limited interior space, was a small luggage rack mounted at the rear. Later (1957-onwards) models incorporated sliding side windows for better ventilation. These improved models displaced 297cc, and the 'big' Isetta 300 was reckoned capable of 65mph and 55mpg. Approximately 162,000 Isetta's had been made by the time production ceased in 1962.


THE CAR OFFERED

This 1957 BMW Isetta, chassis 4994492, is a European-specification example that benefits from an older restoration completed more than a decade ago. The car is presented in a two-tone Coral Red and Ivory color scheme and retains the distinctive styling that made the Isetta one of the most recognizable microcars of the 1950s.

The interior is trimmed in tan upholstery with multicolor plaid cloth seat inserts in shades of red, orange, cream, and brown. Matching tan carpeting and tan interior panels complement the exterior color combination and maintain a period-correct presentation throughout the cabin.

Power comes from a 298cc single-cylinder engine paired with a 4-speed manual transmission. The car is described as remaining mechanically stock, with no known major modifications from original configuration.

As one of the most recognizable European microcars of the postwar era, the Isetta remains celebrated for its compact design, distinctive front-entry layout, and unique driving experience, making it a standout addition to any collection of classic automobiles.

THE EARLY CADILLAC

Founded by Henry Leland and Robert Faulconer, the Cadillac Automobile Company, of Detroit completed its first car in October 1902, the firm's superior manufacturing technology - precision gear cutting was Leland and Faulconer's first specialty - soon establishing it as the foremost builder of quality cars in the USA. In 1901, Olds Motor Works contracted for the supply of Leland-built engines and, when unforeseen circumstances frustrated the plan, Leland and Faulconer formed their own company using funds supplied by two of Henry Ford's ex-backers. An exemplary performer by the standards of the day, the Cadillac's single-cylinder engine - known as 'Little Hercules' - was mounted horizontally on the left beneath the front seat and drove via a conventional two-speeds-plus-reverse planetary transmission and center chain drive to the rear axle. That first 1903 curved-dash Cadillac was re-designated as the Model A after the Model B's introduction for 1904, the B being a more expensive version with box-shaped 'bonnet', pressed-steel frame, I-beam front axle and single transverse front spring. At first Leland & Faulconer supplied only engines, transmissions and steering mechanisms for the Cadillac, before taking responsibility for its entire construction in 1905.

Coachwork design was quickly evolving, and the rear entrance tonneau was soon out dated as Cadillac and others sought to make the rear passenger access more accommodating. For this reason 1905 cars no longer had the provision of the detachable rear part of the bodywork as this wasn't practical with a door on either side of the body.

Priced at $750 to $850, the Model C generally matched the specifications of the other single-cylinder Cadillac offerings, but was a mid-year offering that featured the updated Model F hood and was described by Cadillac as "an accommodation to customers who want a detachable tonneau."


THE CAR OFFERED

According to Cadillac build records and based on the engine number, this 1905 Cadillac was delivered new as a Model F Touring. Finished in Green, it was delivered new to Cook & Stoddard Company in Washington, DC. Cook & Stoddard was the premier Cadillac dealership for politicians, DC-area businessmen, and anyone else looking to be someone in a town where being someone meant something.

The interim history of this Cadillac is not, as of yet, know. By at least 1981, it had entered the collection of Dr. H. Bartholomew Cox of Fort Washington, Maryland. A prolific collector, Dr. Cox was able to help recover 143 binders of unique documents of Thomas Edison's that had been stolen from a federal historical site. His collection focused on books and manuscripts with the capstone being a signature from every individual to have signed the Declaration of Independence—including that of Button Gwinnett. He later expanded his collection to presidential memorabilia and more. Cars were always part of his boundless passions, with this Cadillac joining several others in his collection including a 1910 model that was a high school graduation present.

Dr. Cox is understood to have restored this Cadillac between 1982 and 1984, with an album of photos on file documenting the restoration work. According to marque experts, the car likely started life as a Model F but at some point, the body was either refitted or modified into the current configuration of a Roadster with a detachable Rear Entry Tonneau – a feature unique to the Model C. In 1986, Dr. Cox would sell his Caddy on Christmas eve to a collector in Oslo, Norway. The Caddy would remain in Norway for the next near four score of years before being acquired by the current owner. Most recently the Cadillac has been sent to early car specialist Mark Herman of M.S. Herman & Company for mechanical recommissioning.

While a 1905 Cadillac will not enable entry to the most popular event for early cars, they are nonetheless incredibly sturdy, reliable automobiles that are ideal for the tours orientated to include slightly later examples. In the UK, those include the Singles and Twins events, and the aptly named Creepy Crawly, here in the US the HCCA provides for them well in addition to the recently run Audrain Veteran Car Tour.

THE SILVER SPUR

The Rolls-Royce Silver Spur is the long-wheelbase counterpart to the Silver Spirit and represents one of the last traditionally styled Rolls-Royce saloons before the brand entered the modern BMW-era design language. Introduced in 1980, the Silver Spur combined stately presence, exceptional ride comfort, and hand-crafted luxury in a package aimed at owners who preferred to be driven as much as to drive themselves.

Distinguished by its extended wheelbase, the Silver Spur offered significantly increased rear passenger space, making it especially popular among executives, dignitaries, and luxury chauffeur services. Its classic upright grille, Spirit of Ecstasy mascot, long hood, and restrained body lines embodied the timeless Rolls-Royce aesthetic of the era.

Power came from Rolls-Royce's smooth and torque-rich 6.75-liter V8 engine paired with an automatic transmission, delivering effortless acceleration and near-silent cruising rather than outright performance. The famous self-leveling suspension system provided the "magic carpet ride" Rolls-Royce became known for, prioritizing isolation and comfort above all else.

Inside, the cabin was meticulously finished with hand-selected wood veneers, deep Connolly leather seating, thick carpeting, and extensive sound insulation. Rear passengers enjoyed limousine-like accommodations with generous legroom and an atmosphere designed around comfort and refinement.

Throughout its production run, the Silver Spur evolved through several generations including the Silver Spur II, III, and IV, each bringing incremental improvements in technology, suspension, and interior refinement while maintaining the model's traditional character.

Today, the Silver Spur is appreciated as one of the final truly old-school Rolls-Royces — elegant, imposing, and unapologetically luxurious, with a presence that remains unmistakable decades after its introduction.


THE CAR OFFERED

Purchased new by Hyman Golden, one of the founders of Snapple, chassis no. SCAZN02A6JCX23597 is presented in particularly elegant specification, finished in Acrylic White over a beautifully preserved Tan Connolly leather interior accented by contrasting white piping and complemented by a Tan Everflex roof. The cabin is further enriched by deep-pile Tan Wilton wool carpeting along with exquisitely polished walnut fascia and interior trim throughout. Rear-seat passengers are afforded every luxury, including walnut picnic tables, illuminated walnut vanity mirrors in each rear quarter, carpeted footrests, a folding center armrest, and sheepskin floor coverings. With one-owner and showing just 10,875 miles from new, this Rolls-Royce Silver Spur remains exceptionally well preserved throughout.

Included with this well-preserved 1988 Rolls-Royce Silver Spur are its complete owner's manual set, one set of keys, and the factory-installed, period-correct Motorola mobile phone — a wonderfully evocative feature emblematic of late-1980s luxury motoring.

The mere mention of Rolls-Royce evokes images of timeless elegance, craftsmanship, and opulence, and this Silver Spur embodies those qualities perfectly as a product of one of the marque's most refined and luxurious eras.
