THE 911 GT3 RS

Porsche developed a reputation early on for their surprising performance from their small displacement rear-engine sports and racing cars. These 'giant killers' could outperform cars with much larger engines by making lighter cars with incredible handling. This combination gave Porsches their truly unique driving characteristics and dedicated following of Porsche enthusiasts.

Since the introduction of the original 901 in 1963, Porsche has produced a line of six-cylinder rear-engine sports cars that could compete with much more powerful cars thanks to their low weight and superior handling. The 911 quickly became an icon of performance and handling and offered a driving experience unlike anything else. The 911 has continuously evolved into a more sophisticated, powerful, and capable driving machine, as well as a reliable and usable car.

Starting with the 2.7 Carrera RS, 'RS' variants of the 911 have become coveted for their track readiness, precision and power. With that original RS, a strong formula was developed, involving a distinctive rear wing and aerodynamic enhancements, a potent engine, a stripped-down interior, large side sill graphics, and, importantly, unparalleled performance. Throughout the succeeding generations of 911s, the 'RS' badge remained reserved for only the most hardcore, purpose-built road cars in Porsche's portfolio and have become highly coveted by Porsche collectors and Porsche drivers.

The 997.1 GT3 RS, fits this role extremely well, often considered as being one of the best Porsche wearing the RS prefix. With a large rear wing, large intakes, graphics, and a wide track, the GT3 RS certainly looks the part. The naturally aspirated 6-cylinder engine motivates the GT3 RS to 60 in about 4 seconds, but the car specifically shines through it track performance and handling. Along with stiff springs, solid mounts, and many manually adjustable settings to tune the car to suit the task at hand, one of very few road cars allowed to have these race-derived refinements. Through these manual adjustments and playful 6-speed mechanical gearbox, the GT3 RS forms a formidable track weapon, and canyon carver. True to RS form, it delivers unparalleled performance on and off the track, even for daily duties.

Porsche's GT3 RS continues to set the standard for roadworthy cars with uncompromising on-track performance. Through blending analog adjustments with cutting edge technology and purposeful, lightweight sensibilities with modern comfort and drivability, the GT3 RS provides a unique driving experience in many situations.

The car carries a documented mileage of 33,780 miles, reflecting moderate use consistent with careful stewardship. It features a significant mechanical update with the installation of a 997.2 GT3 Cup-spec 3.8-liter flat-six engine, replacing the original powerplant to enhance performance and reliability.

The exterior has been modified with 997.2 GT3 RS-style rear bodywork and front fender flares, blending factory-correct aesthetics with subtle personalization. The suspension has been upgraded with rebuilt Hlins Clubsport coilovers and adjustable control arms, paired with AP Racing J-Hook rotors and Pagid Racing pads, supporting confident handling and braking performance.

Inside, the cabin retains a factory-correct configuration with carbon-fiber bucket seats upholstered in black leather and Alcantara, complemented by a carbon-fiber center console and body-color interior accents. Additional features include a CAE Ultra Shifter, Rennline alloy pedals, and a MOMO flat-bottom steering wheel wrapped in Alcantara, all contributing to a purposeful driver environment.

The car benefits from a comprehensive service history comprising 18 documented entries, including recent maintenance addressing engine and brake components. It holds a clean CARFAX report and clear titles verified by multiple U.S. states, with no record of accidents or odometer discrepancies. This well-preserved example offers a blend of factory specification and thoughtful mechanical enhancements, appealing to enthusiasts seeking a GT3 RS with both character and performance upgrades.

THE BENTLEY MK VI

As the parent company of Bentley, Rolls-Royce's rationalization policy continued to gather momentum in the aftermath of WWII with the significant introduction of standard bodywork on the Bentley Mk VI, Rolls-Royce's first post-war offering. A separate chassis was retained, featuring a new design with independent front suspension, hydraulic front brakes, and a new 4,257cc, F-head six-cylinder power unit. The engine was enlarged to 4,566cc in 1951, and a much-needed improvement to the standard bodywork arrived mid-way through 1952 in the shape of an enlarged boot together with associated alterations to the rear wings and suspension, subsequent models incorporating these changes were now known as the R-Type Bentley (and E-Series Rolls-Royce Silver Dawn).

The Mk VI four-door standard steel sports saloon was the first post-war luxury car from Bentley. Announced in May 1946 and produced from 1946 to 1952 this very expensive car was a big success for the company. It was also the first car from Rolls-Royce with all-steel coachwork and the first car to be completely assembled and finished at their factory. The decision to offer a complete car with 'in house' bodywork had been dictated by harsh economic reality and 'export or die' was the mantra of British industry in the post-war period. Arguably, the person most responsible for this vital incursion into foreign automobile markets was Government Minister Sir Stafford Cripps, who told British car manufacturers that unless they could guarantee to export 30% (soon rising to 50%) of their products, the government would refuse to supply them with steel. Despite the misgivings of traditionalists, exports rose steadily and, when the home market stabilized, the classically styled 'standard steel' bodywork proved to be entirely acceptable to most potential buyers, making up 80% of total production of this first post-war Bentley. The Mk Vl used the same six-cylinder B60 4 ¼-liter'F-head' straight-six engine as the pre-war Mk V.

THE MINI MOKE

The Mini Moke is one of the most recognizable and unconventional vehicles to emerge from Britain during the 1960s. Originally conceived by the British Motor Corporation as a lightweight military utility vehicle, the Moke ultimately found fame as a fun-loving recreational car synonymous with beach resorts, coastal towns, and carefree motoring.

Based on the mechanical components of the classic Mini, the Mk1 Moke utilized a compact front-wheel-drive layout and lightweight construction that made it nimble, simple, and surprisingly capable. Power came from the dependable Mini-sourced inline 4-cylinder engine paired with a four-speed manual transmission, delivering modest performance but excellent maneuverability and charm.

Distinctive for its minimal bodywork, open-air configuration, and slab-sided styling, the Moke featured removable canvas weather equipment, low seating positions, and exposed simplicity that gave it a character unlike virtually any other vehicle of its era. With no conventional doors and a highly utilitarian design, the Moke perfectly captured the spirit of relaxed leisure motoring.

Though initially unsuccessful in military applications due to its limited ground clearance, the Moke found lasting popularity in resort destinations throughout the Caribbean, Mediterranean, and Australia, becoming closely associated with beach culture and celebrity ownership during the 1960s and 1970s.

Today, early Mk1 examples are especially sought after for their purity of design, charming simplicity, and direct connection to the iconic original Mini. Compact, cheerful, and endlessly charismatic, the Mini Moke remains one of the most beloved cult classics of the British motoring world.

Beaufort's signature visual language — vivid, interwoven abstract forms that evolve into human figures, animals, and flowers — finds an extraordinary canvas in the Moke's clean, unadorned bodywork. The car's simple geometric surfaces and open-air architecture lend themselves naturally to the treatment, allowing the artwork to envelop the vehicle much like a mural inhabits a wall: completely, confidently, and without compromise.

Equal parts collectible automobile and contemporary art installation, this Mini Moke stands as a truly unique expression of creativity and design.

THE MASERATI SHAMAL

Development began with a clear brief: produce a flagship coupé that would sit unambiguously above the Biturbo range, reassert Maserati's sporting credentials, and introduce a proper V8 engine — the first in a Maserati road car since the Indy of the 1970s. Marcello Gandini, fresh from designing the Lamborghini Countach and Diablo, was commissioned to style the body. His result was angular, taut, and unmistakably of the period, integrating Countach-style rear wheel arches.

The Shamal was revealed at Turin in 1990 to considerable attention. The name, following Maserati's tradition of wind names, referred to a hot, dusty north-westerly that blows across Iraq and the Persian Gulf. The press noted the return of the V8, the Gandini styling, and the deliberately exclusive production numbers. It was positioned not as a competitor to the Ferrari 348 — though the comparison was inevitable — but as something more solitary and eccentric.

The Maserati Shamal is one of the more exotic and underappreciated Maseratis of the modern era. Produced from 1989 to 1996, the Shamal was a two-door, 2+2 grand tourer built on a shortened Biturbo platform. Only 369 examples were ever built, making it genuinely rare. They were expensive new and remain a collector's piece today, though values have historically been more accessible than comparable Ferraris of the period.

The heart of the car was a 3.2-liter twin-turbocharged V8, producing around 326bhp — Maserati's first V8 in a road car in quite some time. It could reach 0–60 mph in roughly 5.3 seconds and top out near 170 mph, which was seriously quick for the early '90s.

Unlike modern performance cars, the Shamal demands attention from the driver. Boost comes on hard, the steering is heavy, and the chassis can feel lively under power. Enthusiasts often describe it as charismatic rather than polished.

Like many Maseratis of the Biturbo era, the Shamal has a mixed reliability reputation — maintenance can be complex and expensive. But for enthusiasts, it offers a unique combination of Italian style, a screaming turbocharged V8, and rarity that few cars can match.

Essex pioneered low-cost closed coachwork in the United States, its four-seater sedan being only slightly more expensive than the tourer in 1922, and marginally cheaper by 1925. Essex's big news for 1924 was the switch from four to six cylinders. The new sidevalve power unit started life at an unusually small - for the United States – 130ci in capacity, before being enlarged to 144.5ci part way through the year. Renamed 'Super Six' for 1927, the Essex gained a larger (153.5ci) and more powerful engine that year and four-wheel Bendix mechanical brakes the year after. Stylistically, the Essex looked broadly similar to its Hudson parent, albeit on a smaller scale.

In 1929, the Super Six was renamed the 'Challenger' and tweaked with a beltline that continued around the entire length of the car and a larger radiator shell. To promote the new car, Essex dealers and distributors staged a number of tests in March of '29, calling the event 'National Challenge Week'. Among the many trials was a fuel consumption test in which a Challenger drove 30.5 miles through New York City on 1.5 gallons of gas—no small feat by the standards of then or now!

THE 356 A CARRERA GT

Introduced during the mid-1950s, the Porsche 356 Carrera GT represented the most competition-focused evolution of the marque's already formidable 356 platform. Developed to homologate Porsche's lightweight racing technology for road and rally use, the Carrera GT combined reduced weight, purposeful equipment, and the revolutionary four-cam Type 547 engine derived directly from Porsche's motorsport program.

At the heart of the Carrera GT was Ernst Fuhrmann's sophisticated four-cam flat-four engine, a remarkably advanced design for its era. Compact, high-revving, and mechanically intricate, the engine transformed the 356 into one of the most capable small-displacement sports cars of the 1950s. In GT specification, the Carrera benefited from increased performance tuning and lightweight construction, allowing the model to excel in endurance rallies, hill climbs, and international road racing competition.

Visually understated yet highly purposeful, the Carrera GT could be distinguished by lightweight bucket seats, simplified interior appointments, competition instrumentation, and reduced sound insulation. Beneath its elegant Reutter-built coachwork, the GT offered a uniquely engaging driving experience characterized by sharp handling, remarkable balance, and a free-revving competition engine unlike anything else available in a contemporary production sports car.

Produced in exceptionally limited numbers, the Carrera GT remains among the rarest and most coveted variants of the Porsche 356 lineage today. Its direct connection to Porsche's early motorsport success—including the legendary 550 Spyder and the marque's victories in events such as the Mille Miglia, Targa Florio, and Carrera Panamericana—has cemented the Carrera GT's reputation as one of the most historically significant and desirable early Porsche road cars ever produced.


THE CAR OFFERED


Finished in its rare and highly distinctive factory-correct shade of Aquamarine Blue over black leatherette upholstery with contrasting gray corduroy inserts, this 1957 Porsche 356 A Carrera GT represents one of the most desirable and competition-focused variants of the legendary four-cam Carrera lineage. Produced in exceptionally limited numbers, the Carrera GT was conceived as a lightweight homologation model intended for rallying and international motorsport competition, combining reduced weight with Porsche's advanced Type 547 four-cam engine technology.

According to its accompanying Porsche Kardex warranty record and factory documentation, chassis 101385 was completed on August 9, 1957, and delivered new through Intercaribbean of Cuba to its first owner, a Cuban lawyer and gentleman racing driver. During 1958, the Carrera reportedly enjoyed a successful local competition career, earning numerous victories in period Cuban racing events before being sold and exported to the United States in 1959 through Jacksonville, Florida. Following this early history, the car largely disappeared from public view for several decades before resurfacing in the early 2000s.

Acquired by the current owner as a largely complete restoration project, though without its original engine, the Carrera GT subsequently became the subject of an extraordinarily detailed long-term restoration effort spanning more than fifteen years. Determined to return the car as faithfully as possible to original Carrera GT factory specifications, the owner conducted extensive research throughout the United States and Europe, personally inspecting original Carrera examples while also interviewing former managers from several Porsche factory departments. Additional research was conducted through access to factory records and documentation, much of which was later shared through the 356 Registry. Much of the restoration itself was completed in-house to an exceptionally high standard, with careful attention paid to preserving the authentic appearance, finishes, and competition-focused character of the model.

Most significantly, the current owner undertook a lengthy search for a suitable period-correct four-cam engine, ultimately locating and acquiring the rare Type 547/3 engine no. P90156/666, originally fitted to a 1960 Porsche RS-60 Werks Prototype Spyder, chassis 044. Developed during Porsche's highly successful Spyder racing program, these sophisticated prototype four-cam engines played an important role in the marque's ongoing competition development efforts during the late 1950s and early 1960s. Acquired as a complete and reportedly running engine, subsequent disassembly confirmed that its major components remained original, matching-numbered, providing an exceptional foundation for the project. The inclusion of this historically significant engine greatly enhances the car's appeal and represents an extraordinary companion piece to the Carrera GT.

Over time, the acquisition of the 547/3 engine gradually transformed the owner's vision for the project itself. While the restoration initially focused on returning the GT Coupe as closely as possible to original factory specifications, the owner ultimately embraced a broader philosophy inspired by Porsche's continual pursuit of performance development and engineering advancement. With that spirit in mind, a series of carefully considered period-style enhancements were incorporated without compromising the car's essential design, craftsmanship, or character.

Among the most notable revisions are wider 5.5-inch wheels with burnished aluminum outer rims, instrumentation adapted from a Porsche 904, and a transaxle upgraded internally with later-type 741 racing-oriented components. The Type 547/3 engine itself became the primary focus of the ongoing development program. While preserving its external appearance, numerous internal refinements have been implemented, including upgraded connecting rods and valves manufactured from improved modern materials, along with continued work to enhance the volumetric efficiency of the ports and intake runners. Although final development remains ongoing, performance gains of as much as about 20 percent over original specifications are considered achievable.

While the Type 547/3 engine remains in the process of restoration and final assembly, the car is currently fitted with a fully rebuilt 1,582cc Porsche pushrod engine (Engine no. 751937), installed for testing, tuning, and mechanical sorting purposes. The accompanying four-cam engine is offered largely complete, though requiring final reassembly, dialing-in, and completion work.

Today, chassis 101385 presents as a striking and exceptionally rare example of Porsche's iconic Carrera GT. Combining rare factory colors, fascinating Cuban competition history, meticulous long-term restoration, and the inclusion of a highly significant ex-RS-60 Werks Prototype Spyder four-cam engine, the car represents a remarkable opportunity for collectors seeking one of the most charismatic and competition-oriented Porsche road cars of the 1950s.

THE LOTUS ESPRIT

The Lotus Esprit is one of the most iconic British sports cars ever built — a low, wedge-shaped mid-engine exotic that combined dramatic styling with Lotus' philosophy of lightweight performance and razor-sharp handling.

Produced from 1976 to 2004, the Esprit evolved through several generations while always retaining its unmistakable silhouette. The original Esprit was designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro of Italdesign.
Its sharp wedge profile became one of the defining supercar shapes of the late 1970s and 1980s.
Later redesigns by Peter Stevens modernized the body while preserving the original proportions. Stevens would later design the legendary McLaren F1.

The Esprit achieved worldwide fame in the James Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me
where it transformed into a submarine — one of the most memorable movie cars ever created.
That white Series 1 Esprit became permanently linked to Bond culture and helped elevate Lotus into global recognition.

Over nearly three decades, the Esprit evolved from a lightweight four-cylinder sports car into a genuine supercar contender. Engines included a naturally aspirated inline-4, turbocharged inline-4, and finally the twin-turbocharged V8.

When Lotus closed the Esprit production line in early 2004, it ended one of the longest continuous runs in British sports car history. The 2003 V8 Twin Turbo represents the model at its most complete — the accumulated refinement of nearly three decades applied to a mid-engined platform that had never stopped improving. Peter Stevens' bodywork, penned in 1987, remained as taut and purposeful as the day it was drawn.

The V8 engine was Lotus's own — conceived, engineered, and built at Hethel, a point of considerable pride for a manufacturer of its size. Twin Garrett turbochargers feed a 3.5-liter all-aluminum unit that pulls with authority from low revs and sharpens into something urgent above four thousand.

The V8 powered Esprit was Lotus's answer to critics who felt the four-cylinder Esprit, however tuneable, couldn't compete with Ferrari and Porsche on bragging rights. They proved they could build a proper V8 from scratch — and it sounded magnificent doing it.

The Chassis, true to Lotus philosophy — lightweight, mid-engined, and all about handling. The backbone steel chassis wrapped in a fiberglass body kept weight down to around 1,300kg, meaning the V8 felt every bit as fast as the numbers suggested.

The Esprit ended production in 2004, making the V8 the last and most powerful iteration of a 32-year lineage. It remains one of the most characterful supercars of its era.

Finished in Silver Metallic over Black leather sport seats, the interior consists of an aluminum shift knob, aluminum pedals, silver trim, and a period correct Alpine AM/FM CD player. The car is also equipped with a JRZ suspension and recently installed Nitto tires.

Recent service includes new fuel pumps and spark plugs, as well as a timing belt service. Accompanying the car are multiple keys, owner's manuals, and both removable tops.

Showing just 17,060 miles at the time of cataloging, this 2003 Lotus Esprit V8 represents the most refined iteration of a three-decade icon — built at Hethel, powered by a twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V8, and finished in an era when pop-up headlamps and a razor-edged wedge styling were the language of exotic motoring.

The 2002–2004 Esprit V8 has grown increasingly collectible as the final chapter of a lineage that began in 1976 — nearly three decades of continuous production from a small factory in Norfolk.

THE 993 CARRERA S

For many passionate Porsche collectors and enthusiasts, the 993 generation represents the final chapter in the saga of the air-cooled 911—a culmination of thirty years of relentless refinement, innovation, and German engineering prowess. Introduced for the 1995 model year, the 993 deftly bridged tradition with contemporary design, debuting with sensuous, muscular curves penned by Tony Hatter and a suite of technological improvements that both preserved and advanced the legend of the 911.

Distinctively, the Carrera S variant—offered only in 1997—was conceived as the ultimate grand touring expression for the naturally aspirated, rear-wheel-drive faithful. The C2S was immediately recognizable by its voluptuous Turbo-style bodywork, accentuated by flared fenders, lowered ride height, and wide, aggressive stance. Its clean tail eschewed the ostentatious Turbo rear spoiler, instead opting for a subtler decklid with a split horizontal grille, producing a silhouette of pure automotive poise.

Beneath the surface, the 993 Carrera S was powered by Porsche's revered 3.6-liter, air-cooled flat-six engine producing 282 horsepower—delivering thrilling performance, a full-throated mechanical soundtrack, and the responsive balance beloved by devotees. Mated almost exclusively to a precise six-speed manual gearbox, the C2S retained the quintessential analog character for which the marque is celebrated, offering direct, communicative steering, poised chassis dynamics, and an unmistakable driving experience ungoverned by electronic intervention.

The 993 platform itself was a technological leap forward, featuring all-alloy multi-link rear suspension and a rigorously improved chassis, vastly improving comfort and composure while maintaining the legendary road feel Porsche enthusiasts cherish. The improved Bosch Motronic engine management and sophisticated Bosch ABS braking system gave the Carrera S near-supercar reflexes, while extensive use of galvanized steel protected these rare models from corrosion.

Delivered in a limited run and available for a single model year, the Carrera S soon achieved cult status within the enthusiast community. Its exclusive and evocative specification—defined by wide body, unique options, and rear-wheel drive purity—makes it among the most coveted 993s, an essential keystone for any comprehensive Porsche collection.

The 993 generation remains an inflection point for the 911, marrying the final flowering of air-cooled authenticity with modern build quality and refinement. It stands as a swansong for a classic era—never to be repeated—while its robust engineering ensures continued usability and access to pure driving enjoyment. As appreciation for air-cooled Porsches deepens, the 993 Carrera S persists as a beacon: rare, beautiful, and deeply rewarding.

Today, low-mileage, well-maintained, and factory-original 993 C2S examples are fiercely contested by collectors worldwide, their desirability multiplying not only for their technical merit but their emotional resonance. Few models encapsulate the gestalt of Porsche's identity as powerfully as the Carrera S, making it a perennial highlight in any curated auction roster.

THE ESSEX FOUR

Introduced as a lower-priced companion to the parent Hudson marque in 1919, the first Essex was powered by a four-cylinder, inlet-over-exhaust engine displacing 180 cubic inches (2.9 liters) and producing a class-leading 55bhp. The name soon became synonymous with both high performance and reliability when an Essex averaged over 60mph for 50 hours in December 1919, a stunt which the company followed up by a successful four-car transcontinental trek in 1920. Travelling from San Francisco to New York City, the fastest of the quartet completed its journey in 4 days, 14 hours and 43 minutes.

The company pioneered low-cost closed coachwork in the United States, its two-seater sedan - the cheapest closed car in the USA - being only slightly more expensive than the tourer in 1922 and marginally cheaper by 1925. The Essex was a hit with the buying public. Essex's big news for 1924 was the switch from four to six cylinders, and from then onwards all its models would be sixes.


THE CAR OFFERED

Built toward the very end of production of the Essex Fours, this Touring appears to have been restored several decades ago – likely in the 1970s – and finished in the handsome combination of brown and tan with a brown vinyl interior. Showing well overall, what sets this example apart is the unique and rarely seen roof. Essex did not offer a four-door with a solid roof in 1923, but those wishing for a bit of protection from the elements from find it from a variety of aftermarket producers.

One such company was the Rex Manufacturing Company of Connersville, Indiana. Founded in 1898 as a buggy manufacturer, Rex was swift to recognize the importance of the new horseless carriages and transitioned from building obsolete buggies to weather equipment for vehicles (both horsedrawn and horsepowered) in the form of the Rex Storm Shield. By the teens, Rex had transitioned fully to produced tops and enclosures for automobiles, eventually servicing models from about 50 different manufacturers in the United States – including Essex. When The Great Depression began to eat into the market for new cars, Rex again pivoted – this time to appliances. By 1942, Rex was producing 10% of the refrigerators sold in the United States. Expanding to radio cabinets and enclosures (including for radio magnate and erstwhile vehicle manufacturer Crosley), after WWII Rex became part of Philco and in 1961 was merged into Ford Motor Company.

The rarely seen Rex top on this Essex fully protects the occupants from the outside elements. Fitting tightly onto the bodywork, it has removable window sections that fit onto the top of the doors and B-pillars. Overall, the fit and finish is so nice, one could be forgiving for thinking it came from Essex themselves.

Not often used in recent years, some sympathetic refreshment and recommissioning is recommended before actively touring in this comfortable, all-weather machine.

The W113 SL — introduced in 1963 as the 230SL and developed through the 250SL and 280SL — represented one of the most considered and purposeful sports car designs of the 1960s. Where its predecessor, the spectacular 300SL, had been an engineering statement of near-racing character, the W113 was designed from the outset as a grand tourer of genuine everyday usability, with a fully independent suspension, modern unitary construction, and a cabin of exceptional quality for the period. The car's defining visual element — the concave "Pagoda" hardtop, so called for its resemblance to the tiered roofs of East Asian architecture — was the work of Paul Bracq and served a dual structural purpose, its shape providing additional rigidity while allowing a lower roofline than a conventional convex top would have permitted. The 250SL of 1967–1968 introduced a larger 2,496 cc engine with a seven-bearing crankshaft in place of the 230SL's four-bearing unit, improving refinement and long-distance stamina. Production of the 250SL amounted to just 5,196 cars over two model years, making it the rarest of the three W113 variants and the most distinctive for the collector seeking an unspoiled original or a correctly restored example.

THE PULLMAN 600

"In an age when flaunting your wealth wasn't a crime, the 600 was the automotive equivalent of Monaco. It's a masterpiece of engineering, a quantum leap over its opposition, and redefines the word opulence." - Classic & Sportscar magazine.

By the commencement of the 1960s, Mercedes-Benz's ever-expanding model range was lacking in only one department: a super prestige saloon to rival the Grosser Mercedes of the past. This gap was filled in September 1963 with the appearance at the Frankfurt International Motor Show of the all-new 600. Representing state-of-the-art automotive engineering in just about every department, the supremely well-equipped newcomer featured an overhead-camshaft, fuel-injected, 6.3-liter V8 engine - Mercedes' first - air suspension with variable ride control, four-speed automatic transmission, all-round disc brakes, power-assisted steering, central locking and separate air conditioning systems for front and rear compartments. Its cosseted occupants enjoyed the advantages conferred by multi-way adjustable seating powered by a sophisticated system of hydraulics that also operated the windows and assisted in opening/closing the doors and boot lid. Natural successor to the Mercedes-Benz 300 'Adenauer' limousine, its only credible rival was the Rolls-Royce Phantom V.

The most popular version was the 10.5 foot (3,200mm) wheelbase saloon that could seat up to six passengers, while the long-wheelbase Pullman limousine - a veritable leviathan exceeding 20 feet in length and beloved of Heads of State, not to mention a succession of Popes - could accommodate up to eight. Despite its not inconsiderable weight, the 600 was endowed with highly respectable performance, reaching 62mph (100km/h) in a little under 10 seconds and exceeding 124mph (200km/h) flat out. Only 2,677 examples were made, of which 2,190 were four-door saloons, 428 were Pullman limousines and 59 were landaulettes.

The hinges to the additional doors are still intact and visible. The understated metallic blue exterior is a great fit for this big body Mercedes. Inside, beautiful blue leather graces the drivers compartment while rich, blue velour cloth ensconces the rear cabin. Rich wood trim abounds on the doors, dash, and between the two, rear facing seats where it covers a cooler from which one may pull a bottle of Bollinger or Dom Pérignon upon the consummation of that 'big deal'. The interior presents impeccably well for its age and has been preserved to a high degree.

With such a well-preserved interior and an aged exterior, this Pullman has great "bones" and wonderful potential for a full or partial restoration. This Mercedes is still running its original engine as matched by the data cards. Unquestionably the only car to be loved by everyone from the Hugh Hefner to the Pope and John Lennon to Saddam Hussein, this is the perfect car from which to run an empire—be it business, political, religious, or "other"—from the grand comfort of one of the most legendary luxury cars ever made.

Acceleration was equally extreme: the Diablo vaulted from rest to 100 km/h in just over four seconds, cementing its place among the fastest production cars ever built.

THE AC ACECA

The AC Aceca (pronounced "A-See-Ka") is one of Britain's most elegant and historically significant sports cars.

Introduced in 1954 as the closed-roof sibling to the legendary AC Ace roadster, the Aceca was a masterpiece of British craftsmanship — hand-built with lightweight aluminum coachwork over a tubular steel and ash-wood frame. Its front-end styling reportedly traces back to a design suggested by Pinin Farina for AC in the late 1940s.

One of the Aceca's most notable features was its hatchback at the rear, making it only the second car after the 1953 Aston Martin DB2/4 to incorporate this element.

The Aceca was only slightly heavier than the open Ace, and thanks to better aerodynamics was actually slightly faster, with a top speed of 128 mph. Large 16-inch spoked wheels and near 50/50 weight distribution allowed exceptional handling.

The car originally used AC's own 90 hp, 1,991 cc overhead camshaft engine, but the Bristol-engined Aceca-Bristol was also available from 1956, using a 125 hp unit sourced from Bristol Cars. A small number were later built with a 2.6-liter Ford Zephyr engine.

151 standard Aceca's, 169 Aceca-Bristols, and just 8 Ford-engined models were built when production halted in 1963 — only 328 total.

It's a remarkably rare and beautiful car that sits at the intersection of 1950s motorsport culture and refined grand touring.

THE INDIAN 741

A smaller Indian v-twin, the 37ci (600cc) Scout, joined the 61ci (1,000cc) Powerplus in 1920. The newcomer soon gained a deserved reputation for durability: "You can't wear out an Indian Scout" becoming its advertising slogan. Contributing to this longevity was the use of gears for the primary drive rather than the customary chain, and this unusual feature would endure until 1933. A 45ci (750cc) variant was first offered in 1927 and then in April 1928 the 101 Scout appeared featuring a revised 750cc 'flat head' engine in a new, longer-wheelbase frame. This sporting model would prove an immense success for Indian, so much so that its replacement in 1931 by a heavier Chief-framed model was greeted with dismay. Introduced in 1934, the Sport Scout went some way towards retrieving the Scout's reputation, featuring a lighter 'keystone' (open) frame and European-style girder forks. During WWII's early years, the Scout was produced for Allied forces in 30.07ci (500cc) and 45ci military versions, designated Models 741 and 640 respectively, before the US Army switched to the ubiquitous Jeep for light transportation.
